title: thank-you as a reflex
tomorrow: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds"

lines: GOT THE JOB. DIDN'T GET THE JOB.
cards: Ask a Muslim friend how they are, and there's a good chance the first word back isn't fine. It's alhamdulillah. Got the job?
Alhamdulillah. Didn't get the job? Very often, also alhamdulillah.
Someone sneezes: alhamdulillah. A grandmother, asked about her knees, which are terrible: alhamdulillah. It comes out so fast it sounds like a reflex.
It is one, but a reflex people build on purpose, and the word says more than thanks.

teach.b: Al-hamdu li-llah. Al: the. Hamd: praise.
Li-llah: belongs to God. The praise belongs to God. Not quite thanks, God.
Arabic has a separate word for thanks, shukr, and scholars draw a line between the two. Thanks answers something done for you. Praise answers who someone is.
You can only give thanks for the good day; you can give praise on any day. That's why the word keeps turning up on the bad ones.
The root of hamd, h-m-d, is in a name you know. Muhammad means the one who is praised, again and again. Ahmad, Mahmoud, Hamid: the same three letters.
It's woven into the day. A saying of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ says: when you sneeze, say alhamdulillah, and whoever hears you answers, may God have mercy on you.
After the prayer, many count it thirty-three times, on their fingers or on beads, among other short phrases. And another saying explains why it fits any kind of day.

teach.h: GOOD DAY OR HARD DAY, BOTH COUNT.
teach.b: The believer's situation is a wonder, the Prophet said: when good comes, they're grateful, and that's good for them; when hardship comes, they're patient, and that's good for them too.
Alhamdulillah is the two-second version. It doesn't pretend the bad day was good. It says the praise still belongs where it belonged this morning.

how: Muslims say alhamdulillah when asked how they are, after meals, after sneezing, and at good news and hard news alike; after the prayer many repeat it thirty-three times, counting on their fingers or prayer beads.

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: the root of Muhammad, Ahmad, Hamid

s: alhamdulillah is only for good news
it's said on hard days too. praise answers who God is, not only what went well.
the name Muhammad shares a root with alhamdulillah
h-m-d: Muhammad means the one praised again and again.
hamd and shukr are two words for the same thing
shukr is thanks for something done; hamd is praise for who someone is.

games.q: you sneeze, and say alhamdulillah. a Muslim friend hears you. what does the saying of the Prophet ﷺ say they answer?
o: may God have mercy on you.
games.why: may God have mercy on you: yarhamuk Allah. a sneeze becomes a small exchange of praise and blessing.

practice: Sit comfortably. Bring to mind one thing that went right today, and stay with it. Then one thing that didn't.
Then hold both at once, the good one and the hard one, and notice they belong to the same day. If you want, let the word ride out on a breath: alhamdulillah.

wordCard.voice: Alhamdulillah. The praise belongs to God. Praise, not only thanks, so it fits every kind of day. Eleventh word.

orig.note: Arabic: "the praise belongs to God." al (the) + hamd (praise) + li-llah (to God).

carryVoice: Your line: praise, whatever the day did. It fits the good days and the hard ones. Day eleven.

sources.ref: Qur'an 1:2 (alhamdulillah opens the verse after the bismillah)
Sahih al-Bukhari 6224 (the sneeze and its answer)
Sahih Muslim 2999 (the affair of the believer is a wonder)
